commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Build and distribute signed cross-platform releases
commits.body:
Release automation for the six supported targets, split along the trust
boundary that matters: pull requests build unsigned with no secrets, tags
build signed in a protected environment.

- ci.yml runs tests on Linux, macOS, and Windows, gofmt, shellcheck, the
  installer test, and an unsigned build of every release target. It is
  read-only and reads no secret, so fork pull requests run it unchanged.
- release.yml triggers on tags and manual dispatch only. There is no
  pull_request or pull_request_target trigger, and the Apple secrets are
  scoped to the release-signing environment, so fork pull requests cannot
  reach them. It re-runs the full CI matrix, builds, signs and notarizes the
  macOS pair, re-verifies every artifact after transit, publishes SHA256SUMS
  and a build provenance attestation, and creates the release.
- build-release.sh builds one target, honours SAGA_SIGN_HOOK so signing
  happens before archiving, and injects version, commit, and build date.
- install.sh detects OS and architecture, verifies against SHA256SUMS, fails
  closed when no checksum tool exists, reports the macOS signing authority,
  and installs atomically. It never calls sudo, never strips quarantine, and
  never disables Gatekeeper.
- install_test.sh runs the unmodified installer against a staged release with
  a stub curl, covering tampered archives, missing checksums, missing
  platform builds, and unwritable targets.

macOS signing is optional until the Apple credentials exist: releases build
unsigned with a warning in the notes, and REQUIRE_MACOS_SIGNING=true turns
that into a hard failure once setup is done. docs/releasing.md documents the
process, the six secrets, and the remaining Apple account steps.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Add CDK hosting foundation for shareable sagas
commits.body:
Adds infra/, an AWS CDK v2 app in TypeScript that provisions the hosting
foundation for shareable Review Saga sites. It stops at the boundary:
GitHub OAuth, comment posting, and private saga delivery are documented
extension points, not implementations.

The stack is one CloudFront distribution over two origins. A private S3
bucket holds the generic renderer shell and is reachable only through
Origin Access Control, scoped by AWS:SourceArn to this distribution. An
API Gateway HTTP API fronts a small health/config Lambda at /api/*, so
later authenticated endpoints land somewhere already routed, throttled,
logged, and running under a least-privilege role.

Routing /api/* through the same distribution keeps the browser on one
origin, which is what lets the CSP stay at default-src 'self' with no
CORS and leaves room for a host-only session cookie. Caching is split
three ways: five minutes for shell documents, a year for content-hashed
/assets/*, and nothing for the API. Directory URLs are rewritten by a
CloudFront Function attached to the shell behaviour only; CloudFront
custom error responses would have rewritten genuine API 404s too.

Everything private stays out of the public bucket. Synthesis fails if
the configured shell directory contains saga packages, reserved
overlays, saga manifests, or credential-shaped files - pointing it at
this repository's own review-saga-v2.saga is a test case.

Configuration is CDK context with validation, including the CloudFront
requirement that the certificate live in us-east-1. No domain is
hard-coded and no credential is embedded; the GitHub App secret is
referenced by ARN and granted read on that ARN alone.

infra/go.mod is a shim, not a Go project: it keeps `go build ./...` and
friends from descending into the Go source that npm install leaves
under infra/node_modules.

83 assertion and unit tests pass, and both the default and custom-domain
variants synthesize without warnings. Nothing was deployed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Refine the reviewer into a quiet developer-tool interface
commits.body:
The renderer read like an editorial report: blocky cards, oversized
headings, text buttons repeated per target, and storage vocabulary in the
chrome. This reworks the whole surface toward a tool a reviewer already
recognises from their editor and their code host.

Chrome now speaks the reviewer's language — chapters, files, changes,
comments — and keeps fragment, section, media type, schema, and internal
paths in the CLI and validator where they belong. Authored saga content is
still rendered verbatim and may discuss the format freely.

Compact system UI at 13px, monospace reserved for code and code-shaped
metadata, hairline separators instead of cards, and controls that stay
invisible until the reviewer hovers or focuses the thing they own.

The Saga sidebar becomes a collapsed documentation tree: overview plus
chapters, only the open page expanded into its own headings, with no
fragment counts and no mirror of the on-disk hierarchy. Code Diff keeps a
separate compact changed-file tree with filtering, status, and selection.
Coverage renders as a fully expanded repository tree that keeps its change
and ownership metadata and its bidirectional navigation.

Complete coverage is an invariant, so the success banner is gone. Only
unexplained changes and stale references are reported.

Text controls become icons with tooltips and accessible names, drawn from a
new local SVG sprite that is original to this repository, so a committed
saga still reviews with no network access and no third-party icon licence.
File-type badges cover Go, TypeScript/JavaScript, Markdown, JSON/YAML,
HTML/CSS, SVG/images, shell, and a neutral fallback.

Also fixes four defects found while inspecting the result:

- `.related-chapter>a` matched the excerpt beneath it, rendering prose in
  monospace; the chapter link now has its own class.
- The linked-code drawer chevron was styled by a class the template no
  longer emits, so it never sized or rotated.
- Fragment excerpts ran a heading into the first sentence and kept the
  closing backtick of an inline code span.
- Markdown, text, and licence diffs fell through to the generic keyword
  set, painting every capitalised word as a type. Prose is now left alone.

Deep links, annotation editing, comments, the code drawer, and responsive
behaviour are unchanged. No frontend framework and no CDN.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Add sticky notes as a first-class annotation
commits.body:
A sticky is a new `note` anchor on an ordinary comment thread rather than
a new thread kind. That is the smallest coherent extension: the note keeps
replies, state, permalinks, and Git attribution, and because its visible
text lives in the anchor, rewording is an append-only anchor event instead
of a message rewrite.

The anchor carries plain text (2000 rune cap), a normalized centre point,
and an optional color, all validated in Go and in schema/v2. The overlay
renders note text as a text node only, and an unsafe color falls back to
an accessible default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Harden the E2E suite around identity, session, and accessibility
commits.body:
Fix the two known chrome accessibility defects and the harness gaps that kept
the browser suite from asserting the product's real contracts.

Accessibility:
- The workspace switcher's tablist children are real tabs with explicit
  aria-selected, roving tabindex, aria-controls, matching tabpanels, and
  Arrow/Home/End movement.
- The closed linked-code drawer is inert, so it holds no focusable descendants
  while hidden, and closing returns focus to the control that opened it.
- Scope the aria-pressed layout sweep and the layout click handler to the
  toolbar buttons. The diff surface also carries data-layout, which both put an
  invalid aria-pressed on that container and swallowed every click inside a
  diff before the line-selection and comment handlers could run.
- Give diff rows role=group instead of role=row, which required a table
  ancestor and cell children that do not exist.

Identity:
- Review mutations now refuse a diff URI whose repository is not the one the
  saga declares, for diff reviews and for diff anchors on create and re-anchor.
  The check runs under the writer lock and before any write.

Harness:
- The fixture source repository has an origin matching the declared repository,
  so the suite exercises the identity verification the CLI performs on every
  read instead of being unable to build at all.
- Fixtures expose the comparison identity, canonical diff URI builders verified
  against the server's own rendering, a mutation-token reader, a raw HTTP client
  that can forge Host and Origin, a CLI runner that returns exit status, a
  private server TMPDIR, and whole-tree snapshots for zero-side-effect proofs.
- Add a repositories-only fixture for subprocess tests.

New regressions, each layered at the cheapest honest level:
- Browser: tab semantics, drawer inertness, whole-page axe on every view, and
  commenting on a selected diff line with the exact stored line identity.
- HTTP against the running process: session-token rejection on every mutation
  including a token from another process, cross-origin and foreign-Host
  rejection, malformed/non-canonical/cross-repository diff URIs, upload size,
  count and sniffed-type rejection with staged-file cleanup, and path redaction.
- Subprocess: coverage URI rejection, invalid-saga refusal with zero side
  effects, checkout/origin mismatch refusal, and non-loopback serve refusal.

The code and coverage views still fail axe color-contrast on their muted counts
and metrics. That gap is pinned against an exact rule list rather than excluded
or disabled, so any change to it fails the suite.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Make the public open-source surface publication-ready
commits.body:
Rewrite the README around the actual thesis: a large change should reach a
reviewer as a gradient of information density rather than a flat diff, and a
Change Saga is the material authored to be reviewed — not an AI review. Lead
with the problem, show the authoring loop as a diagram, and keep install and
first-saga instructions short and exact.

Every CLI invocation in the README was executed against a build of this tree in
a scratch repository, including the failure-to-complete path and the exit codes;
the shown status output is real output. Install commands and archive names were
checked against scripts/install.sh, scripts/install.ps1, and
scripts/build-release.sh.

Badges are static and true today. The CI, E2E, and release badges are kept in a
comment with an explanation, because a workflow badge on an unpublished
repository reports nothing and should not be shown until it can.

Add the community health files a public repository is expected to have —
CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, SECURITY.md, SUPPORT.md, GOVERNANCE.md, CHANGELOG.md, issue
forms, and a pull request template — plus a docs index, and expand CONTRIBUTING
with the checks CI actually runs and the rules for changing the on-disk format.
SECURITY.md documents the real posture: loopback-only serving, host validation,
cross-origin rejection, a per-process mutation token, sandboxed fragments, and
what none of that protects against.

Document the versioning policy and release checklist in docs/releasing.md so
CHANGELOG.md and the tag validation in release.yml describe one policy.

Add scripts/check-docs-links.sh, which resolves every relative Markdown link and
heading anchor in the repository offline; all 79 in-repository links pass. No Go
code, schema, or existing workflow was touched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Harden Change Saga schema/runtime integrity
commits.body:
Audit of SPEC.md, schema/v2, the saga loader/validator, the CLI mutation
commands, and target/ID/path resolution, closing the cases where the
published contract and the reference implementation disagreed.

Schema/runtime mismatches. The runtime accepted records schema/v2 rejects:
any "image/*" media type including "image/" and values with spaces or CRLF;
a source.repository carrying URL userinfo, which SPEC.md forbids and which
disagrees with the identity every diff URI builder produces; pr.number 0 and
a relative pr.url; annotation colors outside #rrggbb on text and shape
selectors; negative text anchor positions and stroke widths; and an evidence
file with an empty diffs array, which the schema requires to hold at least
one link. Each is now enforced, pr.number became a pointer so "unset" and an
invalid literal 0 are distinguishable, and the schema gained the entrypoint
and shape-color grammars it was missing. A noncanonical-but-resolvable
repository stays loadable as a warning so existing v2 sagas keep working.

Determinism. SPEC.md resolves thread state, approvals, and reviewed state
from the latest record by created_at, but ties were broken by directory
listing order: two events with the same timestamp made a thread resolve
differently depending on file names. Every append-only record now sorts by
(created_at, id), including the server's latest-wins lookups, and fragments
and messages fall back to path order on equal order values.

Identity and traversal. A thread or message whose directory name disagreed
with its manifest id let the mutation commands and the URN address different
records; both are now rejected, and reply/state/anchor refuse a thread
identifier that is not a stable id rather than silently reducing it with
filepath.Base. Chapter, fragment, landmark, thread, and message entries that
are symlinks or regular files were silently skipped, hiding authored content
behind a valid-looking saga; they are errors now. NaN coordinates passed
every normalized range test and are rejected explicitly.

Windows portability. Entrypoint validation compared filepath.Clean output,
so a nested "assets/app.js" entrypoint authored on Unix was rejected on
Windows. Entrypoints are now slash paths validated OS-independently, with
backslashes, drive letters, control characters, traversal, and reserved
package paths rejected, and non-portable component names reported as
warnings.

Partial mutation. add-chapter, add-section, add-fragment, and init created
directories and wrote manifests in place, so a failure left a manifest-less
chapter or an entrypoint-less fragment that invalidated the saga and blocked
every later mutation. All four now stage into a hidden directory and publish
with one rename, and the authoring commands take the same writer lock the
review overlay uses instead of racing it.

Tests: a schema contract suite that cross-checks every published pattern and
enum against the runtime predicate, adversarial tables for malformed
metadata and symlinked entities, filename-shuffle determinism properties, an
entrypoint fuzz target, and CLI atomicity and concurrency tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Pin and test release archive contents and permissions
commits.body:
Release archives were only ever checked by extracting one and running the
binary. Nothing asserted the shape a consumer actually depends on, and the
member permissions were whatever the builder's umask happened to produce: a
build under `umask 077` shipped a 0700 binary and 0600 documents.

Pin the staged modes in build-release.sh, and add artifact_test.sh, which
builds real tar.gz and zip artifacts and asserts they hold exactly the three
documented members, unpack flat, are all regular files with no setuid, setgid,
or sticky bit, and carry a single-line checksum sidecar that names the archive
by basename and matches it. It also rebuilds under `umask 077` to prove the
modes no longer depend on the build machine.

Modes are read from the archive listing rather than an extraction, because
extraction applies the extracting user's umask and would mask a wrong mode in
the archive itself. The test runs on both the Linux and macOS CI images, since
tar and zip listings differ between GNU and BSD userland.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Make agent authoring ergonomic without loosening coverage
commits.body:
Six concrete pieces of CLI feedback, all of which kept the format's
exact-coverage discipline intact.

Route agents through the query API. install-skill now tells an agent to read
an existing saga only through "change-saga query" and names every operation
with its purpose and usage. The list is generated from the CLI's own dispatch
table, so a new operation cannot ship without appearing in the installed
skill. SKILL.md says the same thing for authoring, not just review.

Add batch coverage. "cover --batch FILE|-" reads newline-delimited JSON
records, or one JSON array, with per-record target/path/side/lines/event/
old_path/new_path/note/name/uris; --target and --note are batch-wide
defaults. The source comparison is read once, every record is resolved before
the first write, and a failing record leaves the saga untouched. Unknown
fields are rejected rather than dropped, because a silently ignored selector
under-covers while reporting success. Batching changes delivery only: each
record still maps the exact atoms it names.

Fix coverage-name collisions. A generated name was slugged as a whole and
truncated to 60 characters, which discarded the uniquifying event ID for any
realistic path. Generated names now keep the uniquifier and are uniquified
deterministically; an explicit --name that is already taken fails with an
error naming the stored file, including when two long names truncate to it.

Stabilize the status contract. The report's collections are always present
and never null, so a complete saga reports "uncovered": []. Diff atoms always
carry "content", including for an empty changed line.

Improve landmark handling. --target accepts <fragment-path>#<landmark-id>,
an unknown landmark lists the ones its fragment declares or says where to
create one, and an unresolvable target names the known targets and points at
"query children".

Fix the help surfaces and add two flags. Every command's -h now leads with
the command actually typed, so "open -h" stops describing serve and
install-skill explains itself instead of printing an empty banner. "cover
--dry-run" reports the records and selectors an invocation would write.
"validate --fix" adds stable anchors to Markdown headings that lack one in
narrative fragments only, preserving existing anchors, fenced code, and line
endings, and never touching append-only review history.

commits.author: trevor@twentyideas.com <trevor@twentyideas.com>
commits.subject: Pin annotation comments to the marks they were drawn on
commits.body:
A comment drawn onto an explanation used to land in the same flat list as a
comment about the whole explanation, so the reviewer had to guess which
rectangle, drawing, highlight, or sticky note a thread belonged to. The
anchor already said which; the renderer just did not use it.

Comments whose anchor is a mark on the content now render as a compact bubble
pinned to that mark, and reveal their thread when the reviewer hovers or
focuses either the mark or the bubble. Replies, resolution, permalinks, and
persistence are the same thread machinery as before. Every other anchor — a
whole fragment, section, chapter, or diff line — keeps exactly the placement
it had; annotationAnchor in server.go is the single place that decides.

The server places each bubble from the stored anchor so the page is right
before script runs, and the browser refines it against the mark as laid out,
which is the only way to place a highlight at all. A revealed comment moves
rather than burying its own mark, and arming a drawing tool closes every open
bubble so the content keeps the pointer.

Labelling the attachment pickers is not incidental: the reply form only ever
reaches an axe scan now that a bubble can be opened during one, and the scan
found them unnamed.
